added_claim_errors: "Scholarships do not" count as compensation is overbroad: W-2 scholarship income and certain taxable graduate/postdoctoral stipends qualify. See [IRS Publication 970](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p970).
"The limits may rise with inflation, which would shorten the schedule" is unsupported: future limits are unannounced, and even $8,000 × 4 = $32,000 still requires five years.
"Complete the transfer by December 31, 2026 to count against the 2026 limit" contradicts the key's April 15, 2027 federal deadline, subject to provider processing.
"Some plans take two to four weeks" supplies an unverified processing range without identifying a plan.
"K-12 tuition (up to $10,000 a year)" is outdated for 2026; the federal limit is $20,000. See [IRS Topic 313](https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc313).

"Subtract that too" after taking the minimum of all limits can understate eligibility: with ample wages, $3,000 eligible funds and $2,000 other IRA contributions, the maximum is min($5,500, $3,000) = $3,000, not $1,000.

"Scholarships ... do not" count as compensation is overbroad: qualifying W-2 scholarship income and certain taxable graduate/postdoctoral stipends count. See [IRS Publication 970](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p970).

The late-2025 survey's "30 states" and detailed state classifications remain unverified here and do not establish 2026 treatment; current [Colorado guidance](https://tax.colorado.gov/income-tax-topics-collegeinvest-contribution-subtraction) explicitly treats these rollovers as nonqualifying.
"He is 22" is not established; someone born in 2004 could still be 21 on the packet's date.
"Completed by December 31, 2026" and "if you miss it, it becomes a 2027 rollover" contradict the key's April 15, 2027 federal deadline, subject to provider processing.
"Form 1099-Q to you as account owner" is wrong for this direct rollover: the designated beneficiary is the recipient. See [IRS Form 1099-Q instructions](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1099q.pdf).

reasons: B narrowly wins because it explicitly accounts for other IRA contributions and is less repetitive; A discusses only other Roth contributions and undermines its five-year schedule with unsupported shortening. Both immediately reject the $48,000 premise, but both give the wrong federal deadline and omit the $40,500 excess calculation and Roth-side 6% excise consequences. B adds a reporting error and a flawed order of operations, while A adds an outdated K-12 limit; neither fully satisfies the key. I recomputed the arithmetic and opened the official IRS and Colorado sources linked above, plus [S. 5550](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-119s5550is/html/BILLS-119s5550is.htm), which supports B's introduction date, proposed change and initial committee referral.
